syllabus.clause: when you still must accept them at the edge and convert immediately

items.item: the last record in a file may or may not have an ending line break
a field is quoted only when it contains a comma, CRLF or quote
an embedded quote is escaped by doubling it
an embedded line break inside a quoted field is legal data
JSON's grammar has one numeric type with no built-in magnitude/precision limit
a double-precision parser only guarantees exact round-tripping for integers in [-(2^53-1), 2^53-1]
JSON text outside a closed ecosystem must be UTF-8
a writer must never prepend a BOM; a reader may tolerate or reject one
CSV has no single formal standard; RFC 4180 documents common practice retroactively, and real producers (e.g. Excel) diverge from it, especially on quoting.
A CSV field is quoted only when it contains a comma, a CRLF or a quote; readers must tolerate quoting applied inconsistently across producers.
An embedded quote inside a quoted CSV field is escaped by doubling it (""), never by a backslash.
RFC 4180 rule 6 makes an embedded line break inside a quoted field legal, so a naive line-based CSV reader corrupts legitimate data.
CSV carries no type system at all: every value is text until a reader infers a type, which is the root cause of classic bugs like a leading-zero ID or postal code being read as an integer.
JSON's grammar has one numeric type ("number"), with no distinction between integer and float; a parser's own choice of representation (commonly IEEE 754 binary64) decides what round-trips exactly.
RFC 8259 states that an integer outside ±(2^53 − 1) is not guaranteed to survive a round trip once real binary64-based parsers are involved, even though the JSON grammar itself has no such limit.
JSON text exchanged outside a closed ecosystem must be UTF-8 (RFC 8259 §8.1); a writer must not prepend a BOM, and a reader may either tolerate or reject one it finds.

A byte order mark (U+FEFF) at the start of a UTF-8 stream is purely a signature with no byte-order meaning in UTF-8 itself, and a parser that doesn't skip it reads it as the file's first, unexpected character.

JSON itself has no per-record delimiter for streaming a sequence of values; JSON Lines (JSONL) is a separate convention — one JSON value per line, UTF-8, no BOM, '\n' as the terminator — layered on top of JSON to make it splittable and streamable.
Neither CSV nor JSON/JSONL supports columnar pushdown: a reader must parse every field of every row to answer even a single-column query, in contrast to the columnar formats later in this chapter.

XML is named by the syllabus as a third text interchange format, more verbose than either CSV or JSON and typically paired with an external schema (XSD/DTD) enforced outside the file itself; this topic names it without building a deep example, matching the syllabus's own brief treatment.
